steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing Omega, an optimistic gradient method that uses an exponential moving average of past gradients for stochastic min-max optimization. Cover the motivation, the problems with existing stochastic extragradient/optimistic methods, what Omega does, and an outline of the paper.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - ML progress: reliably minimizing/maximizing objectives (losses, rewards) with gradient-based optimization
  - min-max relevant: GANs (cite), adversarial training (cite), actor-critic (cite)
  - dynamics understood for minimization, issues for saddle point optimization (cite)
  - stochastic gradient noise can make it worse (cite)

- EG / EFTP
  - Extragradient (cite), extrapolation from the past (cite): popular for deterministic min-max, better convergence guarantees than gradient descent-ascent (cite)
  - stochastic extensions: ISEG (cite), ISOG — can fail on simple stochastic bilinear game, sensitive to noise (cite)
  - concerning for ML: full batch optimization prohibitively expensive

- Alternatives
  - ISEG alternative: same sample for extrapolation + update (cite), converges under weaker assumptions
  - for optimistic gradient, same-sample updates need two gradients per parameter update -> SSOG same cost as same-sample SEG
  - variance-reduced extragradient etc.: mitigate stochasticity issues but much more costly (cite)

- Omega
  - focus on optimistic-like updates
  - Omega = variation of SOG with exponential moving average of historic gradients in update rule
  - mitigates shortcoming of independent samples SOG
  - one gradient computation per parameter update -> better computational complexity than SEG
  - no convergence guarantees; but outperforms SOG on stochastic bilinear games (Figure 1), similar to other methods on quadratic games

- Outline
  - Sec 2: optimistic gradient method
  - Sec 3: Omega + momentum extension
  - Sec 4: general stochastic quadratic games
  - Sec 5: Omega on bilinear, quadratic, quadratic-linear games
  - Sec 6: closing remarks, future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recent progress in machine learning comes from being able to reliably minimize (or maximize) objective functions, like losses or rewards, with gradient-based optimization. Min-max optimization has become especially relevant for machine learning because of the success of GANs, adversarial training, and actor-critic systems. The dynamics of gradient-based methods are well understood for minimization, but some issues come up for saddle point optimization. Also, the noise from using stochastic estimates of the gradients can make the issue worse.

Extragradient and extrapolation from the past are popular methods for solving deterministic min-max optimization problems, because they have better convergence guarantees than gradient descent-ascent. But their natural extensions to the stochastic setting, independent samples stochastic extragradient (ISEG) and independent samples optimistic gradient (ISOG), can fail to converge for a simple stochastic bilinear game and they are sensitive to noise. This is a concern for machine learning applications, where doing full batch optimization is prohibitively expensive.

An alternative to ISEG has been considered where the same sample is used in the extrapolation step and the update step, and it was shown to converge under weaker assumptions. For the optimistic gradient method, though, same-sample style updates would need two gradients to be computed per parameter update. So the same-sample stochastic optimistic gradient (SSOG) has the same computational cost as same-sample SEG. Other methods like variance-reduced extragradient mitigate the issues that come with stochasticity, but they increase the cost of the algorithm significantly.

- Omega
  - focus on optimistic-like updates
  - Omega = variation of SOG with exponential moving average of historic gradients in update rule
  - mitigates shortcoming of independent samples SOG
  - one gradient computation per parameter update -> better computational complexity than SEG
  - no convergence guarantees; but outperforms SOG on stochastic bilinear games (Figure 1), similar to other methods on quadratic games

- Outline
  - Sec 2: optimistic gradient method
  - Sec 3: Omega + momentum extension
  - Sec 4: general stochastic quadratic games
  - Sec 5: Omega on bilinear, quadratic, quadratic-linear games
  - Sec 6: closing remarks, future directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recent progress in machine learning comes from being able to reliably minimize (or maximize) objective functions, like losses or rewards, with gradient-based optimization. Min-max optimization has become especially relevant for machine learning because of the success of GANs, adversarial training, and actor-critic systems. The dynamics of gradient-based methods are well understood for minimization, but some issues come up for saddle point optimization. Also, the noise from using stochastic estimates of the gradients can make the issue worse.

Extragradient and extrapolation from the past are popular methods for solving deterministic min-max optimization problems, because they have better convergence guarantees than gradient descent-ascent. But their natural extensions to the stochastic setting, independent samples stochastic extragradient (ISEG) and independent samples optimistic gradient (ISOG), can fail to converge for a simple stochastic bilinear game and they are sensitive to noise. This is a concern for machine learning applications, where doing full batch optimization is prohibitively expensive.

An alternative to ISEG has been considered where the same sample is used in the extrapolation step and the update step, and it was shown to converge under weaker assumptions. For the optimistic gradient method, though, same-sample style updates would need two gradients to be computed per parameter update. So the same-sample stochastic optimistic gradient (SSOG) has the same computational cost as same-sample SEG. Other methods like variance-reduced extragradient mitigate the issues that come with stochasticity, but they increase the cost of the algorithm significantly.

We focus on methods that use optimistic-like updates. We propose Omega, which is a variation of SOG where the update rule considers an exponential moving average of historic gradients. This helps us mitigate the shortcoming of the independent samples SOG approach. More importantly, Omega only needs one gradient computation per parameter update, so it has better computational complexity than SEG. We do not give convergence guarantees for our approach, but we show that Omega outperforms SOG in stochastic bilinear games (see Figure 1) and has similar performance to other methods for quadratic games.

Outline: Section 2 presents the optimistic gradient method. Section 3 introduces our proposed method, Omega, and also its extension with momentum. Section 4 describes general stochastic quadratic games. Section 5 presents how Omega performs for bilinear, quadratic and quadratic-linear games. Section 6 has closing remarks and future directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The recent progress in machine learning can be attributed to the ability to reliably minimize (or maximize) objective functions, such as losses or rewards, using gradient-based optimization. Min-max optimization has emerged as particularly relevant for machine learning due to the success of GANs [1], adversarial training [2], and actor-critic systems [3]. Although the dynamics of gradient-based methods are well understood for minimization, some issues emerge in the context of saddle point optimization [4]. Moreover, the noise introduced by stochastic estimates of the gradients can exacerbate the issue [5].

Extragradient [6] and extrapolation from the past [7] are popular methods for solving deterministic min-max optimization problems, as they enjoy better convergence guarantees than gradient descent-ascent [4]. However, their natural extensions to the stochastic setting, independent samples stochastic extragradient (ISEG) [8,9] and independent samples optimistic gradient (ISOG), can fail to converge on a simple stochastic bilinear game and are sensitive to noise [5]. This is concerning for machine learning applications, where full batch optimization is prohibitively expensive.

An alternative to ISEG has been considered in which the same sample is used during the extrapolation and update steps [4,10], and it has been shown to converge under weaker assumptions. For the optimistic gradient method, however, same-sample style updates would require computing two gradients per parameter update. The same-sample stochastic optimistic gradient (SSOG) is therefore equivalent to same-sample SEG in computational cost. Other methods, such as variance-reduced extragradient, mitigate the issues associated with stochasticity but significantly increase the cost of the algorithm [5,11].

We focus on methods that employ optimistic-like updates. We propose Omega, a variation of SOG in which an exponential moving average of historic gradients is considered in the update rule. This helps mitigate the shortcoming of the independent samples SOG approach. More importantly, Omega requires only one gradient computation per parameter update, giving it better computational complexity than SEG. Although we do not provide convergence guarantees for our approach, we demonstrate that Omega outperforms SOG in stochastic bilinear games (see Figure 1) and performs similarly to other methods on quadratic games.

Outline: Section 2 presents the optimistic gradient method. Section 3 introduces our proposed method, Omega, and its extension to incorporate momentum. Section 4 describes general stochastic quadratic games. Section 5 presents the performance of Omega for bilinear, quadratic and quadratic-linear games. Section 6 contains closing remarks and future directions.
